# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
# Review: Two-Year Follow-up of the Varden Trial and Halden Subset

This is the strongest document in the series. It takes on most of the open questions raised by the earlier papers:

- **Unrecorded work:** it adds a second hours measure from system logs.
- **The meetings hypothesis:** it tests this under a registration filed before the 24-month outcomes, with baseline meeting data.
- **Durability:** it supplies controlled long-run evidence, which the meta-analysis lacked.
- **The meta-analysis's long-follow-up studies:** it shows they were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours, which supports the doubts about the "no decay" claim.

The Halden subset is caveated honestly as "survivors twice over."

The arithmetic checks out:

| Figure | Calculation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Per hour, timesheets | 0.966 / 0.88 | +9.8% |
| Per hour, logs | 0.966 / 0.89 | +8.5% |
| Halden hours | 34.9 / 40.3 | −13.4% |
| Halden per hour | 96.8 / 0.866 | +11.8% |
| Mediation shares | 47 + 18 + 35 | 100% |

The confidence intervals are consistent with the estimates.

The main issues are that the control group was partly contaminated during the follow-up, that "system log" hours aren't defined, that the mediation result is stated more strongly than the design allows, and that the cost question remains unanswered.

## 1. The control group changed at month 15

Two of the seven control offices cut standing meetings at month 15. Their output per hour then rose 4.1%. This matters for the decay interpretation:

- **The control average rose, so the treated–control gap shrinks for that reason alone.** Two of seven offices gaining about 4% raises the control average by roughly 1.2%, depending on how the 24-month estimate is computed (a final-period snapshot or an average over months 13–24).
- **That could explain a sizeable share of the decline** from 12.5% to 9.8%, possibly close to half of the 2.7-point fall, rather than fading in the treated offices.
- **The decline may therefore overstate decay.** The "some fading" conclusion can't be separated from this without further analysis.

Needed:
- **Report 24-month estimates with and without the two audited control offices.** The intention-to-treat estimate stays primary, but the sensitivity analysis is essential for interpreting decay.
- **Report intermediate estimates (12 and 18 months).** Two time points can't distinguish steady decline from a drop followed by a plateau.
- **Say whether the audits were plausibly prompted by the trial.** Control staff knew a trial was running and could see treated offices cutting meetings, so this may be spillover rather than independent initiative.

The audit is interesting in itself. Treated offices gained about 4 points through meetings (47% of 8.5%) from a relative cut of about 3.3 hours. The audited offices gained 4.1% from a cut of 2.1 hours. These are roughly the same order of magnitude. But it is an uncontrolled before–after comparison in two offices, open to seasonality and regression to the mean, and the authors rightly treat it cautiously.

## 2. Define what "active log-in time" measures

This affects both the hours correction and the mediation result.

- **Are meetings inside or outside the log measure?** If logs capture only time spent working in the case-management system, then meetings, email and phone work fall outside it. In that case:
  - log hours are not "actual hours worked," just a different subset of them;
  - "logs show more work than timesheets" can't be read as capturing unrecorded work in general.
- **The interpretation of the meetings pathway depends on it.**
  - *If log hours include meeting time*, cutting meetings mechanically raises output per hour. That is a real and useful finding (low-value time removed), but it is partly accounting.
  - *If log hours exclude meeting time*, the meetings pathway works through something else, such as fewer interruptions or more focus. That is a different mechanism.
  
  The paper should say which applies.
- **Clarify the levels.** The claim that "Log data show slightly more work" rests on a smaller percentage fall (11% v 12%), not on log hours being higher. Report log hours as numbers, and confirm that pre-period log data exist so the difference-in-differences is valid.
- **Where did the baseline meeting figures come from?** The 9-month report collected meeting data only in month six. The 7.4 and 7.2 hours at baseline presumably come from historical calendars. Say so. This also resolves the baseline-imbalance concern raised earlier: the arms were nearly identical at the start.

## 3. Mediation: "confirms" is too strong

- **The identifying assumption is untestable.** Treatment was randomised, but meeting cuts and fatigue were not. Offices whose managers cut meetings more aggressively may differ in other ways that affect output. The Limitations section acknowledges this. The Summary nonetheless says the test "confirms" that meetings "account for" 47%. Replace with "the registered analysis estimates that…"
- **It is a replication in time, not in units.** The hypothesis came from these same seven treated offices. Registration before the 24-month outcomes is genuinely valuable, but this is a test on the units that generated the hypothesis, not on new ones. "Survives a registered test" is fair; independent confirmation still requires other sites.
- **Inference needs explaining.** The intervals (28–66%, 2–34%) seem tight for 14 clusters. State the method:
  - whether office-months were treated as independent;
  - how clustering was handled;
  - whether small-sample corrections were used, such as a cluster bootstrap with few clusters;
  - whether the two mediators were modelled together, so that their shares can legitimately be added.

## 4. Cost is still missing, and it may be decisive

Timesheet hours fell 12% from a baseline of 37.9, to about 33.4 hours. That is roughly 3.4 hours a week above the 30 scheduled, compared with about 0.4 before the trial. Timesheets record claimed overtime, so treated staff appear to be claiming about 3 extra hours a week, two years running.

- **If that overtime is paid, the cost could be large.** At straight time, 3 hours on a salary covering 30 hours adds about 10% to the wage bill. With a premium it would be more. Combined with output per employee about 3% lower, cost per case could be materially higher than control.
- **Overtime may not be paid.** It might be time off in lieu or banked. The paper should say which and report cost per case closed. That is the figure the county needs for its decision.

The counter-office figure needs its assumptions stated too. Twelve percent more staff raising cost per contact by 9% implies labour is about three-quarters of cost per contact, or some other offsetting assumption. Say what it is.

## 5. The Halden follow-up

- **One reversion doesn't fit the coverage pattern.** The Summary says all three reversions had "client-facing or coverage obligations." The marketing agency cited client deadlines, which the meta-analysis's coding would classify as *discretionary* (output producible any time within a deadline). A discretionary organisation reverting is relevant evidence against a clean split. Report it as such instead of folding it into "coverage obligations."
- **Nine of 23 organisations didn't respond.** Their status is unknown, and non-response is likely to be higher among those that reverted. The reversion rate among the 14 is a lower bound.
- **Check the baseline of 40.3 hours.** It is identical to Varga & Holm's baseline for all 27 time-tracking organisations. Confirm it is the baseline for these 11 organisations specifically, not the average for the larger group.

## 6. Section 5: replies to earlier claims

**Reply to Varga & Holm.** This is largely fair. The 24-month Varden estimate meets every standard they recommended:
- record-based output;
- actual hours;
- randomisation;
- at least 18 months' follow-up;
- all enrolled case-processing offices analysed.

It contradicts "entirely an artifact." Two qualifications:
- **Novelty isn't fully ruled out.** The gain is still declining. "Not consistent with falling to zero by month ten" is correct, but whether it stabilises is open until a later time point (see point 1).
- **The extrapolation was about energy, not output.** Varga & Holm's month-ten extrapolation used Halden's energy scores. My calculation from their figures put the zero point nearer month 9. The rebuttal should make clear it is comparing an output result with an energy extrapolation.

**Reply to the meta-analysis.** This is convincing. Showing that the four long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours removes the basis for "no sign of decay."

**"About a quarter" mixes measures.** Like-for-like on timesheets, the decline from 12.5% to 9.8% is about a fifth. Comparing the 9-month timesheet estimate with the 24-month log estimate (8.5%) gives about a third. Use the like-for-like figure, and note the control-contamination caveat from point 1.

## 7. Minor points

- **Missing intervals.** Sick days, resignations and appeal-overturn rates still have no confidence intervals. Overturns and resignations are still shown as treated v control levels rather than difference-in-differences, as noted at nine months.
- **Primary outcome.** The registered primary outcome is output per FTE: −3.4%, with an interval from −8.0 to +1.2. The Summary includes it, but the per-hour log figure dominates. Lead with the primary outcome.
- **When was the log measure registered?** State whether log hours as an outcome, and output per log-measured hour as the mediation outcome, were specified in the month-11 protocol.
- **Disclosure.** The authors are testing a hypothesis from their own earlier report, and the Halden author is evaluating his own pilot. Registration mitigates this. A brief statement would still be appropriate given that the paper adjudicates published disputes.
- **Appeal overturns.** The 9-month concern about lag no longer applies at 24 months, which is reassuring.

## Overall

The report credibly establishes that, in this setting:
- **A per-hour gain in case-processing persists at 24 months**, of roughly 8–10% depending on the hours measure, with output per employee slightly below control.
- **The counter-office version was unsustainable**, and the county ended it.
- **Meeting reduction is a plausible major pathway.**

Before the conclusions are final, the authors should:
- report the contamination sensitivity and the intermediate time points;
- define the log-hours measure;
- soften "confirms";
- report overtime and cost per case;
- report the marketing-agency reversion candidly.

Earlier I offered a synthesis across the documents. With this follow-up the evidence base is now fairly complete, so I can write a short summary of what the five documents together support, what remains open, and which claims from each have and haven't held up.
